content: 1. Itraconazole and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Close monitoring is required when these drugs are co-administered. Itraconazole may also increase the levels or effects of loperamide through mechanisms involving P-glycoprotein (P-gp). ECG monitoring is recommended, especially if loperamide doses exceed 16 mg/day. 2. Ivacaftor increases loperamide levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Ivacaftor and its M1 metabolite may significantly increase systemic exposure to P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic index. Use caution and monitor closely. 3. Ketoconazole increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 4. Lapatinib increases loperamide levels or effects through P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Lasmiditan increases loperamide levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 6. Lefamulin and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. This combination is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 7. Lenacapavir increases loperamide levels or effects by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Lenacapavir may also increase the risk of adverse reactions to CYP3A4 substrates initiated within nine months of its last subcutaneous dose. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Levoketoconazole increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Lithium and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Lomitapide increases loperamide levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Consider reducing the loperamide dose when used concomitantly with lomitapide. 11. Lonafarnib increases loperamide levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and through P-glycoprotein inhibition. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Lonafarnib is a weak P-gp inhibitor, and dose adjustments of P-gp substrates may be necessary to avoid serious toxicities. 12. Loratadine increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Lovastatin increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Mavorixafor increases loperamide levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition and prolongs the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Mavorixafor causes concentration-dependent QTc prolongation, and dose reduction or discontinuation may be required. Monitor QTc in patients with risk factors for QTc prolongation. 15. Loperamide decreases the levels or effects of intranasal metoclopramide by impairing gastrointestinal motility, which may reduce systemic absorption of metoclopramide. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects. 16. Mirtazapine and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 17. Nefazodone increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Nicardipine increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Nifedipine decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 20. Nilotinib increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 21. Olanzapine and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 22. Osilodrostat and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Oxaliplatin and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 24. Simethicone decreases the levels or effects of pexidartinib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Separate pexidartinib administration by two hours before or after taking a locally-acting antacid. 25. Phenobarbital decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 26. Phenytoin decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 27. Ponatinib increases loperamide levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Primaquine and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 29. Quercetin decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 30. Quinidine increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 31. Ranolazine increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 32. Rifampin decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 33. Ritonavir increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 34. Sarecycline increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor for toxicities of P-gp substrates, and dosage reduction may be required. 35. Sertraline and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 36. Sevoflurane and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 37. Simvastatin increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Siponimod and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 39. Sirolimus increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 40. Solifenacin and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 41. Sotorasib decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, administer sotorasib four hours before or ten hours after a locally-acting antacid. 42. Spironolactone increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 43. St. John’s Wort decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 44. Stiripentol increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Consider reducing the dose of P-gp substrates if adverse reactions occur. 45. Sunitinib and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 46. Tacrolimus increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Tacrolimus and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 47. Tepotinib increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. If co-administration is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage as recommended in its product labeling. 48. Tetrabenazine and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. This interaction is considered serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 49. Tolvaptan increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 50. Trazodone decreases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 51. Tucatinib increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Consider reducing the dosage of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities. 52. Valbenazine and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 53. Vemurafenib increases loperamide levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 54. Verapamil increases loperamide levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 55. Vorinostat and loperamide both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 56. Common adverse effects of loperamide include dizziness, fatigue, headache, abdominal pain, dry mouth, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and pancreatitis. Rare but serious adverse effects include hypersensitivity reactions, bloody diarrhea, high fever, infectious diarrhea, and pseudomembranous colitis. 57. Loperamide should not be used in patients where constipation must be avoided, in cases of abdominal pain without diarrhea, or as primary therapy for acute dysentery (bloody stools and high fever), acute ulcerative colitis, bacterial enterocolitis (caused by Salmonella, Shigella, or Campylobacter), or pseudomembranous colitis associated with antibiotic use. 58. Loperamide is contraindicated in children under two years of age. Chewable tablets should be thoroughly chewed before swallowing. 59. Loperamide is classified as pregnancy category B, while simethicone is category C. It is unknown if loperamide is excreted in breast milk; therefore, caution is advised. Pregnant or breastfeeding patients should consult a healthcare professional before using over-the-counter medications.
